chunks: "Lightning is basically a giant electrostatic discharge between a charged region of a thundercloud and the ground, or another part of the cloud. It starts with charge separation.
Inside a thunderstorm, strong updrafts carry water and ice up past the freezing level.
Small ice crystals collide with heavier soft hail called graupel, and charge gets transferred in each collision.
The light crystals get carried up with positive charge, and the heavier graupel ends up negative in the middle of the cloud.
That leaves a big negative region a few kilometres up, and it induces positive charge on the ground below. When the field gets strong enough, the air breaks down.
A channel of ionized air called a stepped leader works its way down in jumps of tens of metres. As it gets close, the field at tall objects is enough to launch upward streamers.
When one connects, you've got a conductive path, and a huge return stroke flows: tens of kiloamps in a few microseconds.
That current heats the channel to around 30,000 K, which is the flash, and the air expands explosively, which is the thunder.
Usually there are several strokes down the same channel, which is why lightning flickers. For hardware, the takeaway is surges.
Even a nearby strike induces big transients through that huge di over dt , so outdoor electronics need surge protection and good grounding."
